newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions want Schroeder to challenge Kohl.
newsitem.headline: German unions want Schroeder to challenge Kohl.

text.p: Leaders of Germany's trade union movement have urged the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to name Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroder as their candidate to challenge Helmut Kohl for the post of chancellor at next year's general election.
The SPD candidacy for the chancellorship has not yet been decided, but it appears to be shaping up as a choice between party chairman Oskar Lafontaine and Schroeder.

"Schroeder has the best chance of bringing about a change in government because he's a pragmatic politician," Fritz Schoesser, the head of the German Trade Union Federation (DGB) in the southern state of Bavaria, was quoted on Sunday as saying.
"He enjoys a high standing with both workers and business people," Schoesser told the Bild am Sonntag weekly newspaper. "I'm sure I'm not alone in the DFB in my support for Schroeder."

Schroeder is widely seen as something of a maverick, who dares to question German political taboos such as the likely stability of the European Union's planned single currency. But opinion polls show he attracts more support among the German public than Lafontaine.

"If the SPD really wants to bring about a change in government, Schroeder is the best leading candidate," Peter Deutschland, the head of the DGB in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, told Bild am Sonntag.
"He's accepted in all sections of society, including the most conservative groups."
Kohl, chancellor since 1982, has not yet declared his intention to run again at the head of his centre-right coalition. But his allies expect him to do so.
Opinion polls regularly show voters would prefer Schroeder to Kohl but show a much tighter race if Lafontaine were to stand against the veteran chancellor.
Schroeder defies SPD policy on some issues and annnoys traditional leftists by cultivating close relations with big business. But some union officials see this as an asset rather than a problem.

"As trade unionists we've repeatedly had difficulties with Schroeder. But it's exactly his stance towards us that increases his election chances among sections of society which aren't close to the SPD," Gerhard Klein, deputy leader of the white-collar DAG trade union in Lower Saxony, said.
